title: Electronics
blurb: Components and signals for tinkering with microcontrollers.

lessons.title: Components you meet first
lessons.summary: Resistors, LEDs, capacitors and the voltage divider: the parts in every maker kit.

cards.title: Reading a resistor
cards.text:
Resistors are labelled with coloured bands. The first two are digits, the third is a multiplier, and a gold or silver band at the end gives the tolerance.

Black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9.

deep.x: Through-hole resistors are marked with coloured bands instead of printed numbers. Once you know the code, you can read any value in seconds.
Precision resistors use three digit bands, a multiplier and a tolerance band (often brown, ±1%).
The tolerance band (gold or silver) is usually set slightly apart and goes on the right. If in doubt, measure with a multimeter.
Two digits, a multiplier and a tolerance: that's the whole code.

cards.title: Every LED needs a resistor
cards.text: An LED drops a fixed forward voltage (Vf, about 2 V for red, 3 V for white or blue) and will draw as much current as it can get, then burn out. A series resistor takes up the leftover voltage and sets the current.
example: 5 V supply, red LED (2 V), 20 mA

deep.x: An LED has an almost fixed forward voltage. Above it, current rises steeply, so without a limit it burns out. A series resistor sets the current.

x: Red LED on 5 V at 10 mA
White LED on 3.3 V at 5 mA

deep.x: Modern LEDs are bright at 2–5 mA. Using less current saves power and keeps microcontroller pins within limits.

deep.w: Bigger resistor means dimmer and safer
deep.r: yes, but too big and a white LED on 3.3 V may barely light; check the forward voltage

cards.title: Capacitors store charge
cards.text:
A capacitor is two plates separated by an insulator. Connect it to a voltage and charge piles up on the plates until it matches the supply. It charges quickly at first, then slows down.

In practice they smooth out ripples on a power rail and supply short bursts of current, which is why you see one next to almost every chip.

deep.x: A capacitor stores electric charge on two conductive plates separated by an insulator (the dielectric). It resists sudden changes in voltage.
A 100 nF ceramic capacitor close to each chip's power pin is standard practice.
Large capacitors in power supplies can hold dangerous charge after unplugging. Discharge them safely before working inside.
Capacitors are tiny local energy reservoirs.

cards.title: Try it: the voltage divider
cards.text: Two resistors in series split a voltage in proportion to their values. It's the standard way to bring a 5 V or 12 V signal down to the 3.3 V an ESP32 pin can take.

deep.x: Two resistors in series divide a voltage in proportion to their values. It's one of the most common circuits in electronics.

v.f: V out = V in × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2)

deep.x: A divider only works if the load draws little current. A load with low resistance pulls the output down. Microcontroller inputs draw almost nothing, so they're fine.

items.w: Use a divider to power a 3.3 V module from 5 V
items.r: Use a voltage regulator

deep.x: Two resistors, one ratio: the simplest analogue circuit.

cards.title: Standard resistor values
cards.text: Resistors come in standard series rather than every value. The E12 series has 12 values per decade: 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82. Pick the nearest standard value to your calculation.

deep.x: Resistors come in standard series of preferred values, spaced roughly evenly on a logarithmic scale, so each value covers its tolerance range.
Each value is about 21% higher than the previous one in the E12 series, matching ±10% tolerance so the ranges overlap.

x: Choose 330 Ω for an LED (slightly less current)

deep.x: If an exact value is needed, combine two standard resistors in series or parallel, or use E96 precision parts.
Calculate, then round to the nearest standard value.

cards.title: Resistor power rating
example: = 0.06 W: a ¼ W part is fine
cards.text: Resistors turn power into heat and have a maximum rating: common through-hole ones are ¼ W. Check P = I² × R and pick a resistor rated comfortably above it.

deep.x: Resistors convert electrical power into heat. Each has a maximum power rating beyond which it overheats.

items.b: ¼ W (most common), ½ W, 1 W and up

x: = 0.25 W: use at least ½ W

deep.x: Choose a rating at least double the calculated power. A resistor at its full rating can get hot enough to burn fingers or discolour the board.
Check the watts, not just the ohms.

cards.title: Series and parallel resistors
cards.text: In series, resistances add up. In parallel, the total is less than the smallest one; two equal resistors in parallel give half the value.

deep.x: Combining resistors creates new values. Series adds them; parallel reduces the total.
For two resistors in parallel: R = (R1 × R2) ÷ (R1 + R2).
Series adds up; parallel always gives less than the smallest.

cards.title: Capacitor types
cards.text: Ceramic capacitors are small and cheap, used for decoupling (typically 100 nF). Electrolytic capacitors store more (µF to mF) but are polarised: connect them backwards and they can burst.

deep.x: Different capacitor technologies suit different jobs.

items.b: compact, polarised, can fail short if abused

items.r: Match the stripe (−) to the lower voltage

deep.x: Reversed electrolytics can overheat, leak or burst.
Always choose a voltage rating comfortably above the circuit voltage, often 1.5–2× for electrolytics.
Swollen or leaking electrolytic capacitors are a classic cause of failing power supplies and old motherboards.
Ceramics decouple; electrolytics store bulk energy.

cards.title: RC time constant
cards.text: A resistor charging a capacitor takes a predictable time. After one time constant (R × C) the capacitor reaches about 63% of the supply; after five, it's essentially full.

deep.x: When a resistor charges a capacitor, the voltage rises quickly at first, then slows as the capacitor fills. The time constant τ = R × C describes the pace.
Discharging follows the same curve in reverse: after one time constant, 37% of the voltage remains.

cards.title: Inductors
cards.text: An inductor is a coil that resists changes in current, storing energy in its magnetic field. They're key in switching power supplies and filters.

deep.x: An inductor is a coil of wire that resists changes in current, storing energy in its magnetic field.

steps: Switch on: current builds in inductor
Switch off: inductor keeps current flowing

deep.x: Interrupting current through an inductor suddenly produces a high voltage spike, which is why relay coils need flyback diodes.
Inductors are to current what capacitors are to voltage.

quiz.explain: R = (12 − 3) ÷ 0.010 = 900 Ω. You'd pick the next standard value up, 1 kΩ.

quiz.q: Bands brown, black, orange. What's the value?

quiz.explain: Equal resistors split the voltage in half.

quiz.explain: Equal resistors in parallel halve the value.

lessons.title: Signals & microcontrollers
lessons.summary: How a chip like the ESP32 reads and controls the real world.

cards.title: Digital vs. analog
cards.text:
A digital signal has two states: low (0) or high (1, often 3.3 V). An analog signal can be any value in a range, like a temperature sensor's output.

Microcontrollers are digital at heart. To deal with analog they use an ADC to read and PWM to fake an output.

deep.x: Signals are either digital (discrete states, usually 0 and 1) or analogue (continuously variable). Microcontrollers are digital but have tools to handle analogue.

items.b: digital to analogue: true analogue output

deep.x: A voltage near the middle is ambiguous: avoid signals that sit there.
Digital signals survive noise well: a little noise on a 3.3 V "1" is still clearly a 1. That's why digital systems are so reliable.
The world is analogue; computers are digital; converters bridge the gap.

cards.title: PWM: dimming by blinking
cards.text:
Pulse-width modulation switches a pin fully on and off very fast. The fraction of time it's on is the duty cycle. An LED or motor responds to the average: 25% duty on a 12 V supply behaves roughly like 3 V.

It's efficient because the switch is always fully on or fully off, so little energy is wasted as heat.

deep.x: Pulse-width modulation switches a pin fully on and off rapidly. The load responds to the average, so changing the on-time controls brightness or speed.

v.f: Average V = duty cycle × V supply

items.b: above about 1 kHz to avoid visible flicker

deep.x: A switch fully on has little voltage drop, and fully off has no current, so little power is wasted either way.
The LEDC peripheral provides many PWM channels with adjustable frequency and resolution, often used for LED dimming and motors.
PWM fakes an analogue level by switching faster than the load can notice.

cards.title: Pull-up resistors
cards.text:
An input pin connected to nothing 'floats' and picks up noise, randomly reading 0 or 1. A pull-up resistor ties it gently to 3.3 V so it reads 1 by default. Press the button and the pin connects to ground, reading 0.

Most microcontrollers have internal pull-ups you can switch on in code.

deep.x: An unconnected input pin "floats", picking up noise and reading random values. A pull-up or pull-down resistor gives it a defined default state.
A direct wire to 3.3 V would short circuit when the button connects the pin to ground. The resistor limits that current to a fraction of a milliamp.

cards.title: ADC resolution
cards.text:
An analog-to-digital converter turns a voltage into a number. An n-bit ADC has 2ⁿ steps. The ESP32's 12-bit ADC gives 4096 steps over about 3.3 V.

Its readings are less accurate near 0 V and near the top of the range, so keep signals in the middle where you can.

deep.x: An analogue-to-digital converter turns a voltage into a number. Its resolution, in bits, sets how many steps it can distinguish.
For precise measurements, use an external ADC such as the ADS1115 (16-bit).
Taking many readings and averaging them reduces noise and improves effective resolution.
More bits mean finer steps, not necessarily more accuracy.

cards.title: GPIO pins
cards.text: General-purpose input/output pins can be set as inputs (read a button) or outputs (drive an LED). On an ESP32 they work at 3.3 V and can safely supply only a few milliamps each.

deep.x: General-purpose input/output (GPIO) pins are a microcontroller's connection to the outside world. Each can be configured in software.

items.b: keep to about 10–20 mA per pin

deep.x: GPIO pins signal; transistors do the heavy lifting.

cards.title: 3.3 V vs 5 V logic

items.r: divider or level shifter

items.w: 3.3 V pin drives a 5 V relay coil
items.r: use a transistor driver

cards.text: Many modern chips (ESP32, Raspberry Pi) use 3.3 V logic; Arduino Uno uses 5 V. Feeding 5 V into a 3.3 V pin can damage it. Use a voltage divider or level shifter between them.

deep.x: Different boards use different logic voltages. Connecting them directly can damage the lower-voltage chip.

items.w: 5 V sensor output straight into an ESP32 pin
items.r: Use a voltage divider or level shifter

items.b: ESP32, Raspberry Pi, most modern sensors
Arduino Uno, older modules, many relay boards

deep.x: A 3.3 V output often counts as "high" for a 5 V input, but not always. Check the 5 V device's input threshold.
Check the logic voltage before connecting two boards.

cards.title: Interrupts
cards.text: Instead of checking a button thousands of times a second (polling), an interrupt makes the chip jump to your code the moment the pin changes. It saves power and never misses a quick event.

deep.x: Interrupts let a microcontroller respond instantly to events instead of constantly checking for them.

x: Set a flag; do the heavy work in the main loop
Avoid delays, Serial printing and Wi-Fi calls inside them

deep.x: Let hardware call you when something happens.

cards.title: Debouncing

steps: Contacts bounce for a few ms

cards.text: Mechanical buttons bounce: one press produces several rapid on-off pulses in a few milliseconds. Software ignores changes for ~20–50 ms after the first one, or a small capacitor smooths them.

deep.x: Mechanical contacts bounce when pressed, producing a burst of on-off transitions over a few milliseconds. Debouncing filters this so one press counts once.

items.b: resistor and capacitor smooth the signal

deep.x: Libraries like Bounce2 for Arduino, or ESPHome's filters, handle debouncing for you.
One press, one count: debounce every mechanical input.

cards.title: Timers and millis()

items.r: check elapsed time and keep looping

cards.text: Rather than freezing the program with delay(), good code checks elapsed time and does other work meanwhile. This keeps sensors, Wi-Fi and displays responsive.

deep.x: Using delay() freezes the program. Checking elapsed time with millis() lets the program do several things at once.

items.r: if (millis() − last ≥ 1000) { last = millis(), … }

deep.x: millis() overflows after about 49.7 days. Using subtraction (now − last) handles the rollover correctly; comparisons like "now > target" break.
Each task checks whether its own interval has passed.
Never wait when you can check the clock.

cards.title: Microcontroller vs computer
cards.text: A microcontroller (ESP32, Arduino) runs one program directly on the hardware, boots instantly and uses milliwatts. A single-board computer (Raspberry Pi) runs Linux, with more power and complexity.

deep.x: Microcontrollers and single-board computers both run code but serve different purposes.

items.b: 240 MHz dual core, about 520 KB RAM, Wi-Fi
2.4 GHz quad core, up to 16 GB RAM

deep.x: Many projects combine both: microcontrollers handle sensors and timing, a computer runs the dashboard and logic (for example ESPHome with Home Assistant).

quiz.explain: The average of 12 V on half the time is 6 V.

options: Reads randomly because it picks up noise
quiz.explain: With nothing defining its level, the pin picks up stray charge. A pull-up or pull-down fixes that.

quiz.q: How many steps does a 10-bit ADC have?

options: Because the contacts bounce and create several false presses

quiz.q: What's the risk of putting 5 V into an ESP32 input pin?

lessons.title: Diodes
lessons.summary: One-way valves for current, and their many uses.

cards.title: A one-way valve
cards.text: A diode lets current flow in one direction (anode to cathode) and blocks it the other way. The band on the body marks the cathode.

deep.x: A diode lets current flow in one direction (anode to cathode) and blocks it in the other. It's the electronic equivalent of a check valve.
A diode is a junction between p-type and n-type semiconductor. The junction creates a barrier that current can cross easily only one way.
The band marks the end where current exits.

cards.title: Forward voltage
cards.text: A silicon diode drops about 0.6–0.7 V when conducting; a Schottky diode only 0.2–0.4 V, which wastes less power. LEDs drop more: 2 V for red, about 3 V for blue and white.

deep.x: A conducting diode drops a roughly fixed voltage, its forward voltage (Vf). The type determines how much.
Forward voltage falls about 2 mV for each °C rise, which is used in simple temperature sensors.
Every diode costs a little voltage; Schottkys cost less.

cards.title: Reverse-polarity protection
cards.text: A diode in series with a power input stops damage if someone connects the battery backwards. It costs a little voltage; a MOSFET does the same with almost no loss.

deep.x: Connecting a battery backwards can destroy a circuit instantly. A diode or MOSFET in the supply line prevents this.

items.b: almost no loss, slightly more parts

deep.x: A P-channel MOSFET in the positive line, with its gate to ground, turns on only when polarity is correct, dropping just millivolts.
One cheap part can save a whole board from a reversed battery.

cards.title: Rectifiers
cards.text: Four diodes in a bridge turn AC into pulsing DC: both halves of the wave come out positive. Add a big capacitor and it smooths into near-steady DC.

deep.x: Rectifiers convert AC into DC. A bridge of four diodes uses both halves of the AC wave.

items.m: ripple frequency (100 Hz from 50 Hz full-wave)

x: minus two diode drops ≈ 15.6 V DC

deep.x: Switch-mode supplies rectify mains directly and then convert at high frequency, avoiding bulky transformers.
Diodes turn alternating current into a one-way flow.

cards.title: Flyback diodes

items.r: add a diode across the coil, band to +

items.w: transistor dies after a few weeks
items.r: flyback diode fitted

cards.text: When you switch off a relay or motor coil, its magnetic field collapses and creates a voltage spike that can kill the transistor driving it. A diode across the coil safely absorbs the spike.

deep.x: Coils such as relays, solenoids and motors store energy in their magnetic field. When switched off, they produce a voltage spike that can destroy the transistor driving them.

items.w: Relay coil driven with no diode
items.r: Diode across coil, cathode to positive

steps: Voltage spikes to tens or hundreds of volts

items: Fast or Schottky diodes for PWM motors

deep.x: The diode slows the relay's release slightly. For fast release, a Zener in series with the diode is sometimes used.
Every switched coil needs a flyback diode.

cards.title: Zener diodes
cards.text: A Zener diode conducts backwards at a precise voltage, such as 3.3 V or 5.1 V. With a resistor it makes a simple voltage reference or protects inputs from overvoltage.

deep.x: A Zener diode conducts in reverse at a precise breakdown voltage, which makes it useful for references and protection.

steps: Zener holds voltage at its rating

deep.x: A Zener regulator wastes power and only suits small currents. Modern circuits usually use linear or switching regulators instead.
Zener diodes are named after American physicist Clarence Zener, who described the breakdown effect in 1934.

cards.title: LEDs are diodes
cards.text: A light-emitting diode gives off light when current flows forward. The colour depends on the semiconductor material. Long leg is the anode (+), the flat side marks the cathode (−).

deep.x: A light-emitting diode emits light when current flows forward through it. The semiconductor material determines the colour.
LEDs convert electricity to light far more efficiently than filaments and last tens of thousands of hours.
Addressable LEDs such as WS2812 contain a tiny controller, so each LED in a strip can be set to any colour by a microcontroller.
Long leg to positive, always through a resistor.

cards.title: Photodiodes and solar cells
cards.text: Run in reverse, a diode can detect light: photons free electrons and a tiny current flows. Light sensors, remote-control receivers and solar cells are all photodiodes at heart.

deep.x: Diodes can also detect light. Photons free electrons in the junction, producing a small current proportional to the light.
Infrared remotes flash an IR LED in coded pulses, typically modulated at around 38 kHz. A receiver module with a photodiode decodes them.
LDRs are simpler, slower light sensors whose resistance drops in light, common in hobby kits and street-light switches.
Every solar panel is a giant photodiode.

cards.title: TVS diodes
cards.text: Transient voltage suppressor diodes clamp very fast spikes, like static discharge on a USB port or a surge on a long sensor cable, protecting the chip behind them.

deep.x: Transient voltage suppressor (TVS) diodes clamp very fast voltage spikes, protecting sensitive chips from static discharge and surges.
Many products are tested to IEC 61000-4-2, simulating static discharges of several kilovolts.
Ports touched by people need TVS protection.

cards.title: Diodes for OR-ing power
cards.text: Two diodes let a circuit run from whichever supply is higher, such as USB or a battery, without the two feeding into each other.

deep.x: Two diodes can let a circuit draw power from whichever source is higher, such as USB or a battery, without the sources feeding each other.
The higher voltage forward-biases its diode and reverse-biases the other, so only one source supplies the load.
Diode OR-ing lets the stronger supply win automatically.

options: To absorb the voltage spike when it switches off
quiz.explain: The flyback diode protects the driver.

lessons.title: Transistors as switches
lessons.summary: How a tiny signal controls a big load.

cards.title: Why you need one
cards.text: A microcontroller pin can only supply a few milliamps. A motor, LED strip or relay needs far more. A transistor lets the small pin current control a much larger load current.

deep.x: A microcontroller pin can supply only a few milliamps. Motors, relays and LED strips need far more. A transistor lets a small current or voltage control a much larger one.

items.b: high-power switching in drives and EVs

deep.x: Transistors let tiny signals command big loads.

cards.title: BJT: current controls current
cards.text: In a bipolar transistor (NPN), a small current into the base lets a much larger current flow from collector to emitter. The ratio, the gain (hFE), is often 100 or more.

deep.x: In a bipolar junction transistor (BJT), a small base current controls a larger collector current.

steps: Load current flows collector to emitter

x: Need ≥ 1 mA base, use 5 mA to saturate

deep.x: In switching use, drive the base hard enough to "saturate" the transistor, minimising collector-emitter voltage (about 0.2 V) and heat.
BJTs need base current; give them enough to switch fully.

cards.title: MOSFET: voltage controls current
cards.text: A MOSFET is controlled by the voltage on its gate, with almost no gate current. When fully on, its resistance can be just milliohms, so it barely heats up. Most power switching uses MOSFETs.

deep.x: A MOSFET's gate is insulated, so it's controlled by voltage with almost no steady gate current. When fully on, it behaves like a very small resistor.
A BJT dropping 0.2 V at 10 A would waste 2 W, plus base drive power.
MOSFETs switch big currents with almost no control power.

cards.title: Low-side switching
cards.text: The simplest way: put an N-channel MOSFET between the load and ground. The pin drives the gate; when it's high, the load's ground path closes.

deep.x: The simplest MOSFET circuit places an N-channel MOSFET between the load and ground. The microcontroller drives the gate.
An N-channel MOSFET switches on when its gate is several volts above its source. With the source at ground, a 3.3 V pin can drive it directly (with a logic-level part).

items.w: Separate grounds for microcontroller and 12 V supply
items.r: Connect the grounds together

deep.x: The gate voltage is measured relative to the source, so both circuits must share ground.

items: Not for loads that need constant ground
High-side switching needs P-channel or driver

deep.x: Load to positive, MOSFET to ground, grounds connected.

cards.title: Logic-level MOSFETs

items.r: logic-level MOSFET
it's only half on, check gate voltage

cards.text: Many MOSFETs need 10 V on the gate to switch fully on. With a 3.3 V microcontroller, choose a logic-level MOSFET specified to be fully on at 2.5–3.3 V, such as the AO3400 or IRLZ44N.

deep.x: Standard MOSFETs need around 10 V on the gate to switch fully on. With a 3.3 V microcontroller, you need a "logic-level" part specified at low gate voltage.

items.w: IRF540 driven from a 3.3 V pin
items.r: Logic-level MOSFET rated at 2.5–3.3 V

R ds(on) specified at 2.5 V or 3.3 V

deep.x: A MOSFET that's only partly on gets hot, wastes power and may fail, even though the load seems to work.

deep.w: A threshold of 2 V means 3.3 V is plenty
deep.r: the threshold is where conduction starts, not where the MOSFET is fully on

cards.title: Gate resistor and pull-down
cards.text: Add a small resistor (around 100 Ω) between pin and gate to limit current spikes, and a 10 kΩ pull-down from gate to ground so the MOSFET stays off while the microcontroller boots.

deep.x: Two resistors make a MOSFET switch reliable: one limits gate current, the other keeps it off when the pin is floating.
The gate acts like a small capacitor. Charging it suddenly draws a current spike from the pin and can cause ringing. A small series resistor tames this.
A 10 kΩ pull-down holds the gate at 0 V until the pin takes control.
Two cheap resistors prevent mysterious glitches.

cards.title: Transistors as amplifiers
cards.text: Between fully off and fully on, a transistor can amplify: a small varying signal at the input gives a larger copy at the output. That's how radios and audio amplifiers work.

deep.x: Between fully off and fully on, a transistor can amplify: small changes at the input produce larger changes at the output.
Amplifiers need biasing: a steady operating point in the middle of the active region, so the signal can swing both ways without clipping.
Today, most small-signal amplification uses op-amps, which contain many transistors in one chip.
The same transistor can be a switch or an amplifier.

cards.title: Heat in switches
cards.text: Power lost in a switching MOSFET is I² × R(on). A MOSFET with 20 mΩ carrying 10 A loses 2 W, which needs a small heatsink. Switching fast also matters, because power is lost during each transition.

deep.x: Even efficient switches lose some power as heat. Too much heat damages transistors, so it must be calculated.
During each on-off transition, voltage and current overlap briefly, wasting energy. At high PWM frequencies, these losses add up.
R ds(on) rises with temperature, often doubling at high temperatures, so hot MOSFETs lose even more.
Calculate the watts; size the heatsink.

cards.title: Optocouplers and solid-state relays
cards.text: An optocoupler passes a signal through light inside a sealed chip, isolating two circuits electrically. Solid-state relays use the same idea to switch mains loads silently, without moving parts.

deep.x: An optocoupler transfers a signal through light inside a sealed package, electrically isolating two circuits.
Some SSRs switch AC loads only when the voltage crosses zero, reducing electrical noise. They're ideal for heaters, not for dimming.
Light carries the signal; the circuits never touch.

cards.title: Billions on a chip
cards.text: Modern processors contain tens of billions of microscopic MOSFETs acting as switches. The same device that drives your LED strip, shrunk to a few nanometres, does all the computing.

deep.x: Modern processors contain tens of billions of microscopic MOSFETs, each acting as a switch. Computing is billions of these switching billions of times per second.
Moore observed that the number of transistors per chip doubled roughly every two years, a trend that held for decades.
Modern "nanometre" process names (like 3 nm) are marketing labels rather than actual feature sizes, but transistors are only tens of atoms wide in places.
The switch that drives your LED strip, shrunk a billion-fold, runs your phone.

lessons.title: Op-amps
lessons.summary: The Swiss army knife of analog electronics.

cards.title: What an op-amp is
cards.text: An operational amplifier is a chip with two inputs (+ and −) and one output. It amplifies the difference between the inputs by an enormous factor, often 100,000 times or more.

deep.x: An operational amplifier (op-amp) is a chip that amplifies the difference between its two inputs by a huge factor, often 100,000 or more.

items.b: positive and negative or ground rails

deep.x: The term "operational amplifier" comes from 1940s analogue computers, where they performed mathematical operations like addition, integration and differentiation.
An op-amp is a difference amplifier with enormous gain.

cards.title: Feedback tames it
cards.text: On its own, that huge gain is unusable. Feeding part of the output back to the minus input sets a precise, stable gain chosen by two resistors.

deep.x: Raw open-loop gain is too large and unpredictable to use directly. Negative feedback, connecting the output back to the inverting input, sets a precise gain.
The gain then depends only on resistor values, not on the op-amp's variable internal gain. Resistors are precise and stable.
Feedback trades excess gain for precision.

cards.title: Non-inverting amplifier
cards.text: The classic way to boost a small sensor signal. The output follows the input, multiplied by a gain set by two resistors.

deep.x: The non-inverting amplifier boosts a signal without inverting it. The input goes to the + input; two resistors set the gain.

x: Sensor gives 0–300 mV, ADC wants 0–3 V

deep.x: The non-inverting input draws almost no current, so it doesn't load delicate sensors.
Two resistors set the gain precisely.

cards.title: The voltage follower
cards.text: Connect the output straight to the minus input and the gain is 1. Useless? No: it isolates a weak source from a heavy load, a "buffer".

deep.x: Connect the output directly to the inverting input and the gain is exactly 1. The output copies the input, but with much more driving ability.
A voltage divider with large resistors can't drive a load without its voltage dropping. A follower after it holds the voltage steady.
A gain of 1 can be the most useful gain of all.

cards.title: Comparators
cards.text: Without feedback, an op-amp (or a dedicated comparator chip) just tells you which input is higher: output high or low. Great for thermostats and light-activated switches.

deep.x: Without feedback, an op-amp acts as a comparator: its output swings fully high or low depending on which input is larger.
A little positive feedback creates two thresholds, preventing rapid on-off chatter.
Chips like the LM393 are designed for comparison: faster, with open-collector outputs suited to logic.
A comparator answers one question: which is bigger?

cards.title: Two golden rules
cards.text: With negative feedback, analyse op-amp circuits with two rules: no current flows into the inputs, and the output does whatever it takes to make both inputs equal.

deep.x: With negative feedback, op-amp circuits can be analysed with two simple rules, popularised by Horowitz and Hill's classic book "The Art of Electronics".

items: No current flows into the inputs
The output makes both inputs equal

x: Non-inverting amp, input 0.2 V, Rf 9 kΩ, Rg 1 kΩ

deep.x: The enormous open-loop gain means only a microscopic difference between inputs is needed for any realistic output.
Two rules solve most op-amp circuits.

cards.title: Rail-to-rail

items: output stops short of the rails
output reaches near 0 V and 3.3 V

cards.text: Older op-amps can't swing their output close to the supply rails. On 3.3 V or 5 V circuits, choose a rail-to-rail op-amp so the signal can use the full range.

deep.x: Older op-amps can't drive their outputs close to the supply voltages. On low-voltage circuits this wastes much of the range.

x: Loses a third of the ADC range

deep.x: Rail-to-rail input op-amps also accept input signals near the supply rails. Check both input and output specifications.

cards.title: Filters
cards.text: With capacitors, op-amps make active filters: low-pass to remove noise from a sensor, high-pass to block DC, band-pass for a specific frequency.

deep.x: Op-amps with resistors and capacitors build active filters that shape signals by frequency.

items.b: removes one frequency, e.g. 50 Hz hum

deep.x: Filters let through what you want and block what you don't.

cards.title: Summing and differences
cards.text: Op-amps can add several signals (audio mixers) or subtract one from another (measuring the small voltage across a current-sense resistor).

deep.x: Op-amps can add several signals or subtract one from another, building blocks for mixers and measurement circuits.

items.b: precise difference with high input impedance

deep.x: Chips like the INA128 or the HX711 (for load cells) amplify tiny differences while rejecting noise common to both inputs.
Op-amps can do arithmetic on voltages.

cards.title: The 741
cards.text: The μA741, introduced in 1968, became the most famous op-amp ever made and is still taught today, though modern parts are far better for low-voltage circuits.

deep.x: The μA741, introduced by Fairchild Semiconductor in 1968, became the most famous op-amp in history and a staple of electronics education.
The 741 remains in textbooks because its behaviour is well documented, even though modern designs use better parts.
The 741 taught generations of engineers; modern circuits use its descendants.

options: Buffers a weak signal with a gain of 1
quiz.explain: It isolates the source from the load.

lessons.title: Power supplies and regulators
lessons.summary: Getting the right voltage, cleanly and efficiently.

cards.title: Why regulate?
cards.text: Batteries sag as they discharge, and USB can vary between about 4.75 and 5.25 V. Chips want a steady voltage, so a regulator holds it constant whatever the input does.

deep.x: Electronic chips need a stable supply voltage. Batteries sag as they discharge, adapters vary and loads change suddenly. A regulator holds the output steady.

items.b: 4.2 V full to about 3.0 V empty

items: waste the voltage difference as heat

deep.x: Clean, stable power is the foundation of reliable electronics.

cards.title: Linear regulators
cards.text: A linear regulator (such as an LM7805 or AMS1117) burns off the extra voltage as heat. Simple and quiet, but wasteful when the input is much higher than the output.

deep.x: A linear regulator acts like a self-adjusting resistor, dropping the extra voltage and converting it to heat.

v.f: Power wasted = (V in − V out) × I

x: 12 V to 5 V at 0.5 A with LM7805
= 3.5 W of heat: needs a heatsink

items.b: common on ESP32 boards, about 1 V headroom

deep.x: Linear regulators are cheap, simple and produce very little electrical noise, ideal for small currents and sensitive circuits.
Linear regulators turn excess voltage into heat.

cards.title: LDO regulators
cards.text: A low-dropout (LDO) regulator works with input only slightly above output, for example 3.6 V in for 3.3 V out. Essential when running from a single lithium cell.

deep.x: A low-dropout (LDO) regulator keeps regulating even when the input is only slightly above the output, often by just 0.1–0.3 V.

x: Li-ion cell 3.7 V nominal, 3.4 V near empty
Only an LDO can keep working until the battery is nearly flat

deep.x: The current an LDO uses itself matters for battery projects. Some draw milliamps; good ones draw a few microamps.
LDOs are still linear: efficiency is low when the input is much higher than the output.
For battery projects, choose an LDO with tiny quiescent current.

cards.title: Buck converters
cards.text: A buck converter steps voltage down by switching on and off very fast through an inductor. Efficiency of 85–95% means little heat, even from 24 V to 3.3 V.

deep.x: A buck converter steps voltage down efficiently by switching rapidly and storing energy in an inductor.

v.unit: efficiency 24 V to 3.3 V at 1 A, % (approx.)

v.f: V out ≈ duty cycle × V in

items.m: fraction of time the switch is on

deep.x: Because power is conserved (minus losses), a buck converter delivers more current at the output than it draws from the input.

x: 24 V in, 3.3 V out at 2 A (6.6 W)

deep.x: Cheap buck modules (such as those based on MP1584 or LM2596) make it easy to power 3.3 V or 5 V circuits from 12–24 V supplies.
Buck converters step down voltage with little heat.

cards.title: Boost converters
cards.text: A boost converter steps voltage up, such as from a 3.7 V battery to 5 V for USB. It draws more current from the battery than it delivers at the output.

deep.x: A boost converter steps voltage up, for example from a 3.7 V battery to 5 V for USB.

v.f: I in ≈ I out × V out ÷ (V in × efficiency)

x: 5 V at 1 A from a 3.7 V battery, 90% efficient

items.b: either, as battery voltage crosses the output

deep.x: Boosting large ratios draws heavy input currents and reduces efficiency.
Boosting voltage costs extra current from the source.

cards.title: Efficiency compared
cards.text: For a large drop, switching regulators win. For small drops and noise-sensitive analog circuits, an LDO can be better.

deep.x: For a large voltage drop, switching regulators win easily. For small drops and noise-sensitive circuits, an LDO can be the better choice.

items.b: LDO or buck followed by LDO

deep.x: Match the regulator to the voltage drop and noise needs.

cards.title: Ripple and noise
cards.text: Switching regulators leave a small ripple at their switching frequency. Sensitive circuits (audio, precise ADCs) use extra filtering or an LDO after the buck converter.

deep.x: Switching regulators leave small ripple and noise at their switching frequency and its harmonics. Most digital circuits don't care; sensitive analogue circuits might.

steps: Clean supply for ADC or audio

deep.x: An oscilloscope with a short ground spring on the probe reveals ripple accurately; long ground leads pick up extra noise.
Buck for efficiency, LDO for cleanliness, both for the best of each.

cards.title: Choosing a wall adapter
cards.text: Match the voltage exactly, make sure the current rating is at least what your project needs, and check polarity of the barrel plug. A higher current rating is fine: the device only draws what it needs.

deep.x: The right adapter matches voltage and polarity exactly and can supply at least the current needed.
Common barrel plugs are 5.5 × 2.1 mm and 5.5 × 2.5 mm. They look similar but fit poorly if mismatched.

items.w: 12 V adapter on a 5 V device
items.r: Exact voltage match, always

deep.x: Voltage must match; current can be higher.

cards.title: USB power delivery
cards.text: USB-C PD negotiates higher voltages, 9, 15 or 20 V, up to 100 W or more, but only after a digital handshake. A plain USB-C cable without negotiation gives 5 V.

deep.x: USB Power Delivery (USB PD) negotiates higher voltages over USB-C, allowing fast charging of phones and laptops.
A "PD trigger" module can request 9, 12 or 20 V from a USB-C charger, turning laptop chargers into flexible bench supplies.
Cables above 3 A (for 100 W and more) contain a small chip (e-marker) that tells the charger they're rated for 5 A.
USB-C gives 5 V by default; higher voltages need negotiation.

cards.title: Brown-outs

items.r: stronger 3.3 V supply and a 470 µF capacitor near the board

cards.text: If the supply dips below what a chip needs, it can misbehave or reset. ESP32s are famous for resetting on Wi-Fi transmit bursts with a weak supply. A good regulator and a big capacitor near the board fix it.

deep.x: A brown-out is a dip in supply voltage below what a chip needs. It can cause resets, crashes or corrupted data.

items.r: Stronger supply and a large capacitor near the board

deep.x: Wi-Fi transmission causes current spikes of several hundred milliamps. A weak USB cable, thin wires or a small regulator can't keep up, so the voltage dips.
The ESP32 has a built-in brown-out detector that resets the chip safely when voltage falls too low, rather than letting it misbehave.
Random resets are usually power problems, not code problems.

lessons.title: Sensors
lessons.summary: Measuring temperature, distance, motion and more.

cards.title: From the world to numbers
cards.text: A sensor turns a physical quantity into an electrical signal: a voltage, a resistance, a pulse length or digital data. The microcontroller reads it and converts it to real units.

deep.x: A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal that a microcontroller can read and convert into real-world units.
A sensor can show many decimals and still be wrong by a degree.
Sensors are your project's eyes and ears.

cards.title: Temperature sensors
cards.text: Thermistors change resistance with temperature (cheap, analog). The DS18B20 sends digital readings on one wire. The BME280 adds humidity and pressure over I²C.

deep.x: Temperature is the most common thing makers measure. Options range from cheap analogue thermistors to calibrated digital sensors.

items.b: cheap, analogue, needs a divider and maths
temperature and humidity, slower, less reliable

deep.x: Sensors inside enclosures with ESP32s and regulators can read several degrees too high. Mount them away from heat sources, ideally outside the box.
Many DS18B20s can share a single data pin, each with a unique 64-bit address, ideal for multi-zone monitoring.
Place temperature sensors away from your own electronics' heat.

cards.title: Ultrasonic distance

items.m: m/s speed of sound in air

cards.text: Sensors like the HC-SR04 and the waterproof JSN-SR04T send a 40 kHz ping and time the echo. Distance is half the round trip times the speed of sound.

deep.x: Ultrasonic sensors measure distance by timing the echo of a high-frequency sound pulse.

v.f: Distance = speed of sound × echo time ÷ 2

deep.x: Sound's round trip gives the distance.

cards.title: Ultrasonic quirks
cards.text: Speed of sound changes with temperature (about 0.6 m/s per °C), so add temperature compensation for accuracy. The JSN-SR04T has a blind zone of roughly 20–25 cm and needs a clear path.

deep.x: Ultrasonic sensors are simple but have quirks that affect accuracy.

items: Speed of sound changes with temperature

x: Speed changes from about 337 to 349 m/s

deep.x: The JSN-SR04T can't measure closer than about 20–25 cm, because the transducer is still ringing from its own pulse. Mount it high enough above the maximum water level.
Take several readings and use the median to ignore occasional false echoes.
Correct for temperature and respect the blind zone.

cards.title: Motion sensors
cards.text: PIR sensors detect the infrared heat of moving people and animals. Microwave radar sensors detect motion through thin walls and even breathing; they're used for presence detection.

deep.x: Motion and presence sensors trigger lights, alarms and automations when people move.
Passive infrared sensors detect changes in infrared radiation as warm bodies move across their segmented lens. They don't detect people sitting still.
PIR for movement; radar for presence.

cards.title: Light sensors
cards.text: A photoresistor (LDR) is cheap and slow; the BH1750 gives calibrated lux readings over I²C. Useful for automatic lights and blinds.

deep.x: Light sensors measure brightness for automatic lighting, blinds and plant monitoring.
Our eyes perceive brightness roughly logarithmically, so automations often work better with thresholds on a log scale.

items: Face the area you care about

deep.x: Lux values span six orders of magnitude.

cards.title: Current and power sensors
cards.text: A current transformer clamp measures AC current without cutting wires; modules like the PZEM-004T report voltage, current, power and energy. INA219 boards measure DC current and voltage.

deep.x: Measuring current and power lets you monitor appliances, solar output and battery use.

items.b: voltage, current, power, energy via Modbus
DC current and voltage over I²C

items.w: Wiring a mains module without enclosure
items.r: Fully enclosed, properly fused, ideally by a qualified person

deep.x: A current transformer clamps around a single conductor (live or neutral, not both) and produces a small signal proportional to current.

cards.title: Analog vs digital sensors
cards.text: Analog sensors give a voltage you read with the ADC; noise and calibration are your problem. Digital sensors do the conversion inside and send a number over I²C, SPI or one-wire.

deep.x: Sensors either output an analogue signal for the microcontroller's ADC or do the conversion internally and send digital data.

items: noise and calibration are your problem

deep.x: Digital sensors handle long cables better, though I²C itself has length limits. For long distances, use sensors with RS-485 or wireless.
Digital sensors move the hard analogue work inside the chip.

cards.title: Calibration
cards.text: Cheap sensors have offsets and drift. Compare with a trusted reference at two points (for example ice water and room temperature) and correct in software.

deep.x: Cheap sensors often have offsets and gain errors. Comparing them with trusted references and correcting in software improves accuracy dramatically.

x: Fit a line through both corrections

deep.x: ESPHome's calibrate_linear filter lets you enter measured and true values; it applies the correction automatically.
Two good reference points beat a datasheet's typical values.

cards.title: Sampling and averaging

items: Sample only as often as needed

cards.text: Take several readings and average them, or use a median to ignore outliers. Don't sample faster than you need: it wastes power and adds noise.

deep.x: How often and how you sample affects accuracy, noise and power consumption.

items: Sample only as fast as needed

deep.x: Sending readings every second creates millions of data points a year. Reporting only meaningful changes keeps databases lean.
Sample as often as the physics changes, not as fast as the chip can.

options: It detects changes in infrared heat from movement

options: AC current without cutting the wire

lessons.title: Talking between chips
lessons.summary: UART, I²C and SPI explained.

cards.title: Why buses?
cards.text: Sensors, displays and memory chips need to exchange data with the microcontroller. Standard serial buses send bits one after another over a few wires.

deep.x: Microcontrollers talk to sensors, displays and memory through serial buses that send bits one after another over a few wires.
Standard buses let parts from different manufacturers work together, so a BME280 from one company talks to an ESP32 from another.
A few wires and a shared protocol connect everything.

cards.title: UART
cards.text: UART uses a TX line and an RX line, crossed between devices (TX to RX). Both sides must agree on the speed, such as 9600 or 115200 baud. GPS modules and serial consoles use it.

deep.x: UART (universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter) uses one line to send and one to receive, with no shared clock.

steps: Device B RX; Device B TX

deep.x: Both sides must agree on the baud rate in advance. Common rates: 9,600 and 115,200 baud.

items.b: 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit

items.w: Connect RS-232 (±12 V) directly to an ESP32
items.r: Use a level converter such as MAX3232

deep.x: TTL-level UART uses 3.3 V or 5 V; old PC serial ports use RS-232 levels.
Cross TX and RX, match the speed, share ground.

cards.title: I²C
cards.text: I²C uses two lines, SDA (data) and SCL (clock), shared by many devices. Each device has an address, such as 0x76 for a BME280. Both lines need pull-up resistors.

deep.x: I²C (Inter-Integrated Circuit), developed by Philips in 1982, uses two shared lines to connect many devices.
Lines are open-drain: devices pull them low, resistors pull them high. Typical values are 2.2–10 kΩ; many breakout boards already include them.
Two wires, many devices, each with its own address.

cards.title: SPI
cards.text: SPI uses a clock, data out, data in and a chip-select line per device. It's fast, often tens of MHz, so it's used for displays, SD cards and flash memory.

deep.x: SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) uses separate lines for clock, data in, data out and a chip-select for each device. It's fast and simple.
SPI often runs at tens of megahertz, much faster than I²C, which suits displays, SD cards and flash memory.
SPI has four modes defining clock polarity and phase. Controller and device must use the same mode.
SPI trades extra wires for speed.

cards.title: Choosing a bus
cards.text: I²C for many slow sensors on two wires; SPI for speed; UART for modules with their own protocol; one-wire for long chains of temperature sensors.

deep.x: Each bus suits different needs. Many projects use several at once.

items.b: GPS, modems, devices with their own protocol

deep.x: Let the device and distance choose the bus.

cards.title: Address clashes

items.r: change one to 0x77 with its address jumper
add an I²C multiplexer

cards.text: Two I²C devices with the same address can't share a bus. Many boards have a jumper to change the address, or you can use an I²C multiplexer.

deep.x: Two I²C devices with the same address can't share a bus: both would answer at once.

items.w: Two BME280s at 0x76 on one bus
items.r: Set one to 0x77 with its address jumper

deep.x: The ESP32 has two hardware I²C controllers and can assign them to almost any pins, so two buses are easy.

cards.title: I²C scanner
cards.text: When an I²C device doesn't respond, run a scanner sketch that tries every address and lists what answers. No answer usually means wiring, power or missing pull-ups.

deep.x: When an I²C device doesn't respond, an I²C scanner tries every address and lists those that acknowledge.

items.b: device not powered or wrong voltage

deep.x: Setting "scan: true" in the I²C configuration logs all found devices at boot.

cards.title: Cable length
cards.text: I²C was designed for short connections on one board; beyond about a metre it becomes unreliable. For longer runs use RS-485, CAN or a differential bus extender.

deep.x: I²C was designed for short connections on a single board. Long wires add capacitance that slows signal edges until communication fails.
For metres to kilometres, use RS-485, CAN or put a microcontroller near the sensor and send data wirelessly.
I²C is for centimetres, not metres.

cards.title: RS-485 and Modbus
cards.text: RS-485 sends data as the difference between two wires, which rejects noise over long cables. Industrial devices, energy meters and solar inverters often speak Modbus over RS-485.

deep.x: RS-485 sends data as the voltage difference between two wires, making it highly resistant to noise over long cables.

items.b: up to 32 standard loads on one bus
daisy-chained bus with terminators at both ends

deep.x: Modbus, created by Modicon in 1979, is a simple protocol widely used in industry. Energy meters, solar inverters and heat pumps often speak Modbus RTU over RS-485.
An ESP32 with a cheap RS-485 module can read these devices into Home Assistant.
Differential signalling shrugs off noise over long cables.

cards.title: Logic analysers
cards.text: A cheap USB logic analyser records the bits on a bus and decodes them into readable bytes, showing exactly what's being sent. It's the fastest way to debug a stubborn sensor.

deep.x: A logic analyser records digital signals and decodes protocols into readable data, showing exactly what's on the wires.
Inexpensive USB logic analysers with 8 channels at around 24 MHz, used with open-source software like PulseView (sigrok), handle most hobby buses.
When a bus misbehaves, look at the actual bits.

quiz.explain: I²C uses data and clock lines.

What's best for a 300 m cable to an energy meter?
quiz.explain: RS-485 is differential and handles long runs.

lessons.title: Wireless links
lessons.summary: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee and LoRa compared.

cards.title: The trade-off triangle
cards.text: Every wireless technology balances range, data rate and power use. You can't max out all three: long range and low power means very little data.

deep.x: Every wireless technology balances range, data rate and power consumption. Improving one usually costs another.

items.b: slow, short range, very low power
very slow, long range, low power
medium speed, long range, moderate power plus fees

deep.x: Sending more bits per second requires more signal relative to noise. At long distances, signals are weak, so only low data rates get through reliably.
Pick two: range, speed or low power.

cards.title: Wi-Fi
cards.text: Wi-Fi offers high speed and connects directly to your network and the internet, but uses a lot of power. Good for mains-powered devices like cameras and smart plugs.

deep.x: Wi-Fi offers high data rates and direct internet access, but uses significant power, best for mains-powered devices.
Wi-Fi on batteries is possible with deep sleep: wake, connect, send, sleep. Connecting takes time and energy, so readings every few minutes work better than every second.
Wi-Fi is fast and familiar, but thirsty.

cards.title: Bluetooth Low Energy
cards.text: BLE sends small amounts of data over short distances with very little power. Fitness bands, sensors and beacons use it, often running for a year or more on a coin cell.

deep.x: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) sends small amounts of data over short distances with very little power.

items.b: up to 2 Mbps, typically much less
months to years on a coin cell

deep.x: Many BLE sensors simply broadcast readings in advertising packets without connecting, saving power. ESP32 boards can listen and forward them to Home Assistant as Bluetooth proxies.
BLE trades speed for years of battery life.

cards.title: Zigbee and Thread
cards.text: Mesh networks for smart homes: each mains-powered device relays messages, extending range. They need a hub or coordinator, and battery sensors last years.

deep.x: Zigbee and Thread are low-power mesh networks for smart homes, built on the IEEE 802.15.4 radio standard.

items.b: IP-based, used by Matter, needs border router
application standard over Thread or Wi-Fi, launched 2022

deep.x: Battery sensors on Zigbee or Thread can last years, because they sleep most of the time and send tiny messages.
Mesh networks get stronger as you add mains-powered devices.

cards.title: LoRa
cards.text: LoRa uses a special chirp signal to reach several kilometres with tiny power. Data rates are only hundreds of bits to a few kilobits per second: perfect for occasional sensor readings at remote sites.

deep.x: LoRa uses a special chirp spread-spectrum radio technique to send small amounts of data over long distances with very little power.

items.b: hundreds of bits to a few kilobits per second
a few to tens of bytes
higher means longer range, slower data

deep.x: With high-altitude balloons and line of sight, LoRa links have reached hundreds of kilometres.
LoRa whispers a few bytes across kilometres.

cards.title: LoRa vs LoRaWAN
cards.text: LoRa is the radio. LoRaWAN is a network protocol with gateways and servers, like The Things Network. Point-to-point LoRa between two boards needs no network at all.

deep.x: LoRa is the radio technology. LoRaWAN is a network protocol that uses LoRa radios with gateways and network servers.
The Things Network is a community LoRaWAN network with gateways worldwide, including in Portugal, free for fair use.
Two LoRa boards can talk directly, for example a sensor at a farm well sending to a receiver in the house, with no network needed.
LoRa is the radio; LoRaWAN is the network.

cards.title: Frequencies in Europe
cards.text: LoRa in Europe uses the 868 MHz licence-free band, with duty-cycle limits (often 1%), so each device may only transmit a small share of the time.

deep.x: LoRa uses licence-free radio bands, which differ by region. In Europe, it uses the 868 MHz band with duty-cycle limits.

items.l: maximum transmit time per hour at 1%

deep.x: Shared licence-free bands need fairness. Limiting each device's transmit time stops any one device from hogging the airwaves.

x: One message takes about 0.4 s at a slow spreading factor

cards.title: Antennas matter
cards.text: A good antenna, mounted high and clear of metal, often doubles range more cheaply than more power. Never transmit without an antenna connected: it can damage the radio.

deep.x: A good antenna, well placed, often improves range more than extra transmit power, and more cheaply.
Transmitting without an antenna can reflect power back into the radio chip and damage it.
Long, thin coaxial cables lose signal at high frequencies. Keep cables short or use low-loss types.
Raise the antenna before raising the power.

cards.title: Line of sight
cards.text: Radio waves at these frequencies are blocked by hills, buildings and water. In the countryside, raising the antenna a few metres can turn no signal into a solid link.

deep.x: At the frequencies used by Wi-Fi, LoRa and similar radios, signals travel best in straight lines. Obstacles weaken them dramatically.
Radio signals need more than a thin line of sight: an elliptical zone around the path should be mostly clear for full strength.
Height is the cheapest range booster.

cards.title: Cellular IoT
cards.text: Where there's no Wi-Fi or gateway, LTE-M and NB-IoT modules send small amounts of data through the mobile network with low power, for a monthly SIM fee.

deep.x: Where Wi-Fi and gateways are unavailable, cellular IoT technologies send small amounts of data over mobile networks with low power.

items.b: tiny data, deep indoor coverage, very low power

deep.x: A data SIM for IoT costs a small monthly fee, often a few euros, with low data allowances.
Older 2G and 3G networks are being switched off in many countries, so new designs should use LTE-M, NB-IoT or 4G.
Cellular IoT works anywhere there's mobile coverage, for a monthly fee.

quiz.explain: LoRa offers long range at very low power.

lessons.title: ESP32 and ESPHome
lessons.summary: Building smart-home devices without writing much code.

cards.title: The ESP32
cards.text: A cheap microcontroller with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth built in, two cores at up to 240 MHz and dozens of GPIO pins. It's the heart of countless DIY smart-home devices.

deep.x: The ESP32 is a low-cost microcontroller from Shanghai-based Espressif Systems, with built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. It's at the heart of countless DIY and commercial smart devices.
The ESP8266 (2014) became popular when makers discovered it could be programmed directly. The ESP32 followed with more power, Bluetooth and better peripherals.
Many smart plugs, lights and appliances contain ESP chips, which is why hobbyists can often re-flash them with open firmware.
A powerful, connected microcontroller for the price of a coffee.

cards.title: ESPHome in one idea
cards.text: Instead of writing C++ code, you describe your device in a YAML file: which board, which sensors on which pins. ESPHome builds the firmware and connects it to Home Assistant.

deep.x: ESPHome lets you build firmware for ESP32 devices by describing them in a YAML file instead of writing C++ code.
ESPHome was created by Otto Winter in 2018 and is now maintained under the Open Home Foundation, alongside Home Assistant.
Describe the device; ESPHome writes the program.

cards.title: A temperature sensor in YAML
cards.text: A few lines describe the board, Wi-Fi and a sensor: platform dht, pin GPIO4, name "Living room temperature", update interval 60 s. That's the whole program.

deep.x: A complete ESPHome device can be just a few lines. The structure is the same for most sensors.
Store Wi-Fi passwords in a separate secrets.yaml file and reference them with !secret, so you can share configurations safely.
A few lines of YAML replace hundreds of lines of code.

cards.title: Over-the-air updates
cards.text: After the first USB flash, ESPHome updates devices over Wi-Fi. Change the YAML, click install, and the device on the ceiling updates itself.

deep.x: After the first flash over USB, ESPHome updates devices wirelessly. You change the YAML and install from anywhere on the network.

items.b: boots into recovery after repeated crashes

deep.x: Keep enough free flash space for OTA: the device stores the new firmware before switching.
Flash once by cable, then update forever over Wi-Fi.

cards.title: Native API
cards.text: ESPHome devices talk to Home Assistant through a fast native API, with encryption. Entities appear automatically, and automations can run on the device even if Home Assistant is down.

deep.x: ESPHome devices communicate with Home Assistant through a fast native API, with optional encryption.
When a device is adopted, its sensors and switches appear in Home Assistant automatically, with names and units.
ESPHome devices can run automations on the device itself, so a thermostat or light switch keeps working even if Home Assistant is offline.

steps: Reports to Home Assistant when available

deep.x: The API ties devices to Home Assistant; on-device automations keep them independent.

cards.title: UART devices: the AC example
cards.text: ESPHome can talk to appliances over UART. Projects like MitsubishiCN105ESPHome connect an ESP32 to the CN105 port of a Mitsubishi air conditioner for local control without the cloud.

deep.x: ESPHome can talk to appliances over UART. Community projects let an ESP32 control air conditioners, heat pumps and more without cloud services.
This open-source project connects to the CN105 service port on many Mitsubishi indoor units, giving local control of mode, temperature and fan from Home Assistant.

items.b: some ports carry 12 V or 5 V

deep.x: Many appliances already have a serial port waiting for an ESP32.

cards.title: Choosing pins carefully

items.w: analog sensor on an ADC2 pin
items.r: use an ADC1 pin (32–39)
move it to a safe pin

cards.text: Some ESP32 pins are input-only (34–39), some affect boot (0, 2, 12, 15), and ADC2 pins can't be used for analog readings while Wi-Fi is on. Check a pinout before wiring.

deep.x: Not all ESP32 pins are equal. Some have restrictions that cause boot failures or broken features.

items.w: Button on GPIO12 stops the board booting
items.r: Avoid strapping pins for inputs held at boot

items.b: used by flash memory, don't use
unavailable for analogue while Wi-Fi is on

deep.x: Each ESP32 variant (S3, C3, C6) has its own pin restrictions. Always check the specific board's pinout.

cards.title: Deep sleep in ESPHome
cards.text: Battery devices can wake up, take a reading, send it and go back to deep sleep for minutes. A deep-sleep ESP32 draws microamps instead of tens of milliamps.

deep.x: Deep sleep turns off most of the ESP32, leaving only a tiny timer running. Battery devices wake, measure, send and sleep again.
Many development boards draw milliamps even in deep sleep because of their USB chips and regulators. For long battery life, use boards designed for low power.

x: Wake every 10 min, 5 s at 150 mA

deep.x: Deep sleep turns months of battery life into a design choice.

cards.title: ESP32 variants
cards.text: The family keeps growing: ESP32-S3 adds AI instructions and USB, ESP32-C3 is a low-cost RISC-V version, ESP32-C6 adds Wi-Fi 6 and Thread/Zigbee radio.

deep.x: The ESP32 family has grown into many variants, each optimised for different needs.

items.b: Wi-Fi 6, BLE, Thread and Zigbee radio

items: Matter and Thread: C6 or H2

deep.x: Espressif's newer chips increasingly use the open RISC-V instruction set instead of the older Xtensa cores.
ESPHome supports most variants, though newer chips may have fewer community examples at first.
There's an ESP32 for almost every connected project.

cards.title: Local and private
cards.text: ESPHome devices work entirely on your network, with no cloud account. If the internet goes down, your sensors and switches keep working.

deep.x: ESPHome devices work entirely on your local network, with no cloud accounts. Your data stays at home and devices keep working without internet.
Several smart-home companies have shut down cloud services over the years, leaving devices useless. Local control avoids this.

x: Put IoT devices on a separate network or VLAN

deep.x: If it runs locally, it keeps running.

options: They can't be read while Wi-Fi is active

lessons.title: From breadboard to PCB
lessons.summary: Prototyping, soldering and making it permanent.

cards.title: Breadboards
cards.text: A breadboard lets you build circuits without soldering. Holes in each short row of five are connected; the long rails along the sides carry power and ground.

deep.x: A solderless breadboard lets you build and change circuits quickly. Spring clips under the holes connect components in groups.

items.b: 5 holes connected, either side of the centre gap
power and ground along the sides

deep.x: DIP chips straddle the centre gap so each pin gets its own row of four free holes for connections.

items.w: Assuming the whole rail is connected end to end
items.r: Check: some long boards split the rails in the middle

items: Red for power, blue or black for ground

deep.x: Breadboards are for experimenting, not for permanent projects.

cards.title: Jumper wires and loose contacts

items: Check every wire is pushed in

cards.text: Breadboards are great for testing but contacts get loose and add resistance. If a circuit behaves strangely, push the wires in again before rewriting your code.

deep.x: Breadboard contacts loosen with use, and long jumper wires add resistance, noise and confusion.

items.a: Works on the bench, fails later

deep.x: Breadboards add capacitance between rows. Fast signals (tens of MHz) and radio circuits behave poorly on them.
Before blaming your code, wiggle the wires.

cards.title: Soldering basics
cards.text: Heat the joint (pad and wire together) with the iron, then feed solder into the joint, not onto the iron. A good joint is shiny and shaped like a small volcano.

deep.x: Soldering joins metal parts with a molten alloy that wets both surfaces and forms an electrical and mechanical connection.

items.w: Melting solder on the iron and dabbing it on
items.r: Heat the joint, feed solder into the joint

deep.x: Solder flows towards heat. If the pad and lead are hot, solder wets them properly.
Flux cleans oxide from the metals so solder can flow. Most electronics solder has a flux core; extra flux helps with tricky joints and SMD work.
A good joint is shiny, smooth and concave, like a small volcano.

cards.title: Iron temperature
cards.text: For common lead-free solder, around 330–370 °C works well; leaded solder melts lower. Too cold gives dull, grainy joints; too hot burns pads and flux.

deep.x: The right iron temperature depends on the solder, the joint size and the tip.

items.b: burnt flux, lifted pads, oxidised tip

deep.x: Large pads and ground planes soak up heat. Use a bigger tip rather than turning the temperature up a lot.
The EU's RoHS directive has restricted lead in most electronic products since 2006.

cards.title: Bad joints
cards.text: A cold joint looks dull and lumpy and may crack. A bridge connects two pads by accident. Too little solder leaves a weak joint. Desoldering braid or a pump fixes most mistakes.

deep.x: Most soldering problems come in a few recognisable forms, and most can be fixed.
Clean pads, fresh flux and the right tip size prevent most problems.
Reheat, add flux, try again: most joints can be saved.

cards.title: Perfboard
cards.text: Perfboard (stripboard) makes a project permanent without designing a PCB: components soldered in a grid, connected with wire or copper strips.

deep.x: Perfboard and stripboard make a circuit permanent without designing a printed circuit board.

steps: Draw layout on paper or software

deep.x: If you need several copies, compact size or reliability in vibration, design a PCB instead.
Perfboard turns a breadboard prototype into something that lasts.

cards.title: Designing a PCB
cards.text: Free tools like KiCad let you draw the schematic and then the board layout. Upload the files to a PCB maker and boards arrive in about a week for a few euros.

deep.x: Designing your own printed circuit board has become accessible: free software, cheap manufacturing and fast shipping.
Small two-layer boards from online manufacturers can cost a few euros for five copies, with delivery in about a week. Assembly services can even solder the SMD parts.
A PCB turns a tangle of wires into a reliable product.

cards.title: Surface-mount parts
cards.text: Most modern parts are surface-mount (SMD): tiny, soldered onto pads rather than through holes. Sizes like 0805 are manageable by hand; smaller ones need hot air or a reflow oven.

deep.x: Most modern components are surface-mount devices (SMD), soldered onto pads on the board's surface rather than through holes.
0805 is the sweet spot for hand-soldered SMD.

cards.title: Enclosures
cards.text: Projects need a box: IP-rated enclosures for outdoors, 3D-printed cases for custom fits. Plan for cable glands, ventilation and antenna placement outside metal boxes.

deep.x: A good enclosure protects the circuit, the user and the environment, and affects how well the project works.

x: Heat from regulators builds up in sealed boxes
Metal boxes block Wi-Fi and LoRa: put antennas outside
Condensation forms inside sealed outdoor boxes; vents with membranes help
Sensors need contact with the air they measure

deep.x: Plan the box before you finish the circuit.

cards.title: Safety while soldering
cards.text: Use a stand for the iron, ventilate or use fume extraction (flux fumes irritate the lungs), wash hands after handling solder, and wear eye protection when clipping leads.

deep.x: Soldering is safe with simple precautions.
The visible smoke is mostly vaporised flux, which can irritate the lungs and cause occupational asthma with long exposure. Use a fan or fume extractor.
Lead isn't vaporised at soldering temperatures, but it can be ingested from hands. Don't eat at the bench, and wash hands.

items.b: cool under running water for 20 minutes

deep.x: Respect the iron, ventilate the fumes, wash your hands.

quiz.explain: The joint must be hot enough to melt it.
